only a loop repeats its body. | | mis:if_statement->IfRequiresElse | wrong rule: Every if statement requires an else. | right rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional. | | mis:if_statement->IfWaitsForCondition | wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. | right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; Edges offered: | edge | |---| | mis:control_flow->CodeAfterIfSkipped | wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. | right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way. | | mis:control_flow->FalseConditionRestartsProgram | wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. | right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement. | | mis:control_flow->FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode | wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. | right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:control_flow->IfConditionWatched | wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). | right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch. | | mis:control_flow->IfWaitsForCondition | wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. | right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it. | | mis:control_flow->LoopImpliedByOneTest | wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. | right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop. | | mis:control_flow->NoShortCircuit | wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them) | right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramEndsAfterLoop | wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. | right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramLooksAhead | wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. | right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them. | | mis:control_flow->ReturnDoesNotExitLoop | wrong rule: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values. | right rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass. | | mis:control_flow->StatementsRunInAnyOrder | wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. | right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom. |

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | lvl:control_flow@L0#0 | level L0 way everyday_reading: Folk meaning: in everyday instructions a listener reads the whole list at once, does steps in a sensible order and infers what the writer wants. (here mixing in: "Statements in a program can run in any order") | | lvl:control_flow@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: Control flow is the order in which a program's statements are executed (statement sequencing); conditionals and loops are the statements that change it. | | lvl:control_flow@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: Without control statements every statement executes once, in the order given; a block executes its statements in order from first to last; if/if-else choose between one or two alternatives and loops repeat statements depending on a condition. | | lvl:control_flow@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: Execute the statement at the current point; when it completes normally, control passes to the next statement in the block. An if evaluates its condition once and then runs at most one branch; a loop evaluates its condition before each pass; after an if or a loop finishes, control continues with the statement after it. | | lvl:control_flow@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: The output is the sequence of print statements that control actually reaches, in the order reached: e.g. TenHellos prints 1st, 2nd, 3rd Hello once each, then 4th to 10th Hello from the loop. | | lvl:control_flow@L2#2 | level L2 way one_step_execution: One step executes the single statement at the current control point using the current values, updates at most the variables it assigns, and moves the control point to the next statement (or, for an if/loop test, to the chosen branch, back to the test, or past the statement). | | lvl:control_flow@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: Control flow is defined over statements: statements are executed for their effect, and if/while/for are themselves statements that may be used wherever a statement is allowed, so they can nest. | | lvl:control_flow@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: An if changes the default top-to-bottom flow: its condition is tested once when control reaches it, its block runs only if true, and in both cases control then continues with the next statement. | | lvl:control_flow@L3#2 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A flowchart draws control flow: each path through the diagram is a possible path of execution, with a decision box for each if or loop test. | | lvl:control_flow@L3#3 | level L3 way purpose_of_the_whole: Plan: control flow lets one program do different things for different inputs (selection) and do a thing many times (repetition), so a short program can specify a potentially unlimited number of executed statements. | | lvl:control_flow@L4#0 | level L4 way predict_a_change: Reordering two statements generally changes the result whenever one reads a variable that the other writes (e.g. swapping x = x + 1 and print(x));
